title: Think of what you have
hook: count your best things and think how you'd miss them (Meditations 7.27)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kin, wrongdoers seen as those who misjudged. Your line was kin who stumble. Were you able to wish someone well? Day five hundred ninety-one.

The power goes out for a day, and suddenly a light switch is a miracle. You get the flu, and for a week you'd give anything to taste food again. A friend moves away, and the Tuesday coffee you took for granted becomes the thing you miss. We tend to notice what we have at the exact moment it's gone. Marcus Aurelius tried to move that moment earlier, on purpose, while the lights are still on.
screen: `THE POWER GOES OUT.` → `THE TUESDAY COFFEE.` → `NOTICING TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: First, the turn of attention. In Meditations seven, twenty-seven, Marcus tells himself not to dwell on things he doesn't have as if they were already his. Instead, think of what you do have. The mind easily runs to the gap: the bigger apartment, the better job, the life on someone else's feed. Marcus turns the head around. Second, the exercise. From the things you have, he says, pick out the best ones. Then think how eagerly you'd go looking for them if you didn't have them. That's the whole practice, and it's sneaky. It uses the mind's hunger for what it lacks, and points it at what's already in the room. Your knees that work. The person who texts you good night. A quiet morning. Picture them gone, and watch their value rise. Third, the guardrail. Here's what makes it Stoic. Marcus adds a warning right away: be careful that you don't get so attached to these things that you'd be thrown into turmoil if you lost them. So he isn't telling himself to cling. He's asking for something balanced. Treasure them fully. Hold them loosely. Fourth, the shape of it. Other paths have their own practices of thanks, each with its own reasons. What stands out in Marcus's version is that both halves come together: value what you have as if it were gone, and don't be shaken if it goes. Grateful and unafraid at once.
screen: `NOT WHAT YOU LACK.` · `PICK THE BEST YOU HAVE.` · `HOW YOU'D SEEK THEM IF GONE.` · `TREASURE FULLY, HOLD LOOSELY.` · then, large: `WHAT I HAVE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Name three things you have that you'd miss terribly. A person, a body part that works, a place, a small daily pleasure. Take them one at a time. Picture each one gone, briefly, just long enough to feel how you'd long for it. Then let it come back, here, still yours today. Notice any gladness. Then loosen your grip, gently, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Think of what you have. Marcus's exercise: choose your best things and imagine how you'd seek them if they were gone, without clinging. Today's word.
screen: `THINK OF WHAT YOU HAVE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what I have. Today, when you notice yourself wanting something you don't have, name one thing you do have that you'd miss. Day five hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes practice 7.27 by naming a few good things they have and imagining their loss, while reminding themselves not to cling.
